summary: Defines a set of management objects for fault, configuration and performance management of applications from a system's viewpoint, in an SNMP management database. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is a standard set of questions a manager can ask about programs running on a machine, like which are running and how they are doing.

questions: how to monitor applications with snmp
what is the system application mib
what is the default sysappl poll interval
subtitle: An SNMP MIB that lets a manager see which applications are installed and running on a host, without changing the applications.

tldr.problem: Managers need basic fault, configuration and performance information about application software on a host, but most applications have no management support built in.
tldr.mechanism: The System Application MIB models applications as collections of files and executables and exposes three groups: what is installed, what is running or has run, and a map from process IDs back to applications. Everything it reports can be found from the system itself.
tldr.outcome: It gives a generic, system-level view of applications on one host, and expects more detailed application-specific MIBs to refer back to it.

today: RFC 2287 is a Proposed Standard published in February 1998. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2287 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for fault, configuration and performance management of applications from a systems perspective. The objects are restricted to information that can be determined from the system itself, without special instrumentation inside the applications.

The RFC defines an application as one or more units of executable code and other resources, installed on a single host, that a manager can treat as one object. The aim of the system-level approach is ease and speed of implementation, with room for future growth. The abstract also states that the memo does not specify a standard for the Internet community, even though the document is on the Standards Track.
sections.eli5: Programs on a computer are like tools in a toolbox. This document lets a manager ask what tools are in the box and which ones are being used, without the tools needing to say anything.

sections.title: Place in Application Management
sections.content:
The RFC expects more MIB modules to appear over time. This one presents the most general case: generic information whose values can be found from the computer system alone. A finer-grained "appl MIB" is planned for the future, which would need instrumentation in the application. Any link between the two should be made by references from the more detailed MIB back to the sysAppl MIB, and application-specific MIBs such as a WWW MIB should likewise reference back to the generic ones.

The module is sysApplMIB, placed at mib-2 54, and is defined with the SNMPv2 framework documents such as RFC 1902.
sections.eli5: This is the basic, all-purpose layer. More detailed layers can be added later for particular programs, and they point back to this basic one.

sections.title: The Three Groups of Objects
sections.content:
The MIB models application packages as a whole and also the individual elements (files and executables) that make them up. Its objects fall into three groups:

  • System Application Installed: sysApplInstallPkgTable lists installed packages and sysApplInstallElmtTable lists their component files and executables.
  • System Application Run: sysApplRunTable, sysApplPastRunTable, sysApplElmtRunTable and sysApplElmtPastRunTable, plus scalars that restrict table sizes.
  • System Application Map: sysApplMapTable, which maps a known process ID back to the invoked application, installed element and installed package.

For an application to count as installed, its existence and its files must be discoverable without instrumenting it. That may need conventions such as a central installation mechanism or registry. The RFC's examples are the pkgadd utility on many UNIX systems and the global registry on many PC systems.
sections.eli5: There are three notebooks. One lists the programs that are installed, one lists the programs that are running or have run, and one tells you which program a running job belongs to.

sections.title: Running and Past-Run Tables
sections.content:
Each time an application is invoked, a new entry is created in sysApplRunTable, one per invocation, so a package invoked several times has several entries. When the instance terminates, its entry is deleted from that table and a corresponding entry is added to sysApplPastRunTable, which keeps a history.

The element tables work the same way for processes. sysApplElmtRunTable lists every running process, including ones that belong to no identified application, because that shows the full load on the system. When a process ends, it moves to sysApplElmtPastRunTable only if it was part of an identified application, so short helpers like ps or grep show up while running but are not kept as history.

Because the past-run tables keep growing, scalars limit them. sysApplPastRunMaxRows caps the number of entries and sysApplPastRunTblTimeLimit caps their age, with the oldest removed first. The element table has matching sysApplElmtPastRunMaxRows and sysApplElmtPastRunTblTimeLimit scalars. In all, seven scalars control the size of the past-run tables.

To tell when an invocation starts and ends, an agent can use sysApplInstallElmtRole, which marks which element is the primary executable, which must be running for the application to be running, and which depend on others.
sections.eli5: When you start a program it gets a line on the 'running now' list. When it stops, the line moves to a 'ran before' list, and the old entries are cleared out when the list gets too long or too old.

sections.title: Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Implementing this MIB on popular operating systems can take considerable processing power, and it can be hard to know when an application or process starts or finishes. The RFC therefore describes a polling agent: it checks the managed resources at regular intervals, updates a cached copy of the MIB, and answers SNMP requests from that cache. The scalar sysApplAgentPollInterval lets the manager set the polling frequency, with a default of 60 seconds. That keeps overhead low while giving usable information for long-lived processes. A manager should adjust it if short-lived processes matter or if the agent uses too many resources.

The RFC also describes a rare collision in sysApplElmtPastRunTable. It is indexed by the invocation ID and a process-based index, and process numbers can wrap and be reused. If the same invocation runs a second process with a reused number before the old entry ages out, the new entry replaces the old one.
sections.eli5: The computer checks on its programs once a minute by default and writes down what it saw. Check more often to catch quick programs, but that costs more effort.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: To implement this MIB, an agent must make management information available about logical and physical entities in the managed system, and some environments may consider that information sensitive. The RFC suggests that an administrator may want instance-level access control, configuring the access mechanism (such as community strings in SNMPv1 and SNMPv2C) so that certain instances are excluded from particular MIB views.
sections.eli5: A list of everything running on a computer can be private. So the manager of the computer can choose which lines each person is allowed to see.
